title: Coordinate Geometry
prerequisites: Plotting points in the Cartesian plane.

topics.title: Distance Formula and Its Applications
topics.quick_summary: The distance between two points is √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²], which lets geometric properties be verified by calculation rather than by drawing.
topics.real_life: A delivery app computes straight-line distance between two map coordinates with exactly this formula before choosing a route.

detailed.definition: The distance between points A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) is AB = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]. It is the Pythagoras theorem applied to the horizontal and vertical differences.
detailed.key_idea: Because the differences are squared, the order of subtraction does not matter. Distance is therefore always positive, whichever point is taken first.
detailed.working_principle: To classify a figure, compute all sides and both diagonals. Equal sides with equal diagonals give a square; equal sides with unequal diagonals give a rhombus.
applications: Collinearity: three points are collinear if the sum of two distances equals the third.
Circumcentre: the point equidistant from all three vertices of a triangle.
Type of triangle: equilateral, isosceles, scalene or right-angled, from the side lengths.

points: Distance from the origin to (x, y) = √(x² + y²).
Equal sides and equal diagonals → square; equal sides, unequal diagonals → rhombus.
Equal diagonals with unequal adjacent sides → rectangle.
Three points are collinear if AB + BC = AC for some ordering.
mistakes: Subtracting the coordinates in mixed order, e.g. (x₂ − x₁) with (y₁ − y₂).
Forgetting to square the differences before adding.
Concluding a figure is a square from equal sides alone, without checking the diagonals.
topics.memory_hook: 'Difference of x, difference of y, square, add, root' — Pythagoras in coordinates.
topics.advanced: The formula extends unchanged to three dimensions by adding (z₂ − z₁)², and to n dimensions by adding one term per coordinate. It is the Euclidean metric that defines distance in any dimension.

formulas.name: Distance Formula
formulas.variables: (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) = the two points.
formulas.when_to_use: For lengths of sides and diagonals, and for classifying figures.
formulas.common_mistakes: Mixing the order of subtraction between the x and y terms.
formulas.shortcut: The order does not matter because the differences are squared.

topics.title: Section Formula and Area of a Triangle
topics.quick_summary: The section formula locates the point dividing a segment in a given ratio, and the area of a triangle can be found from the coordinates of its vertices alone.
topics.real_life: Placing a milestone exactly two-fifths of the way along a road between two towns is a section formula calculation.

detailed.definition: The point P dividing the join of A(x₁,y₁) and B(x₂,y₂) internally in the ratio m₁ : m₂ has coordinates [(m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁+m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁+m₂)].
detailed.key_idea: The cross-pairing in the section formula is what students most often get wrong: m₁ multiplies x₂, not x₁. Checking the formula against the mid-point case (m₁ = m₂) catches the error instantly.
detailed.working_principle: The area formula gives zero exactly when the three points are collinear, which makes it the standard test for collinearity.
applications: Area zero → the three points are collinear.

points: Mid-point is the special case m₁ : m₂ = 1 : 1.
Centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 from the vertex.
Area = 0 is the test for collinearity.
mistakes: Pairing m₁ with x₁ instead of x₂ in the section formula.
Omitting the modulus and reporting a negative area.
Reversing the ratio when the question specifies the order of the points.
topics.memory_hook: 'Cross the ratio over: m₁ goes with x₂' — and check it reduces to the mid-point when m₁ = m₂.
topics.advanced: The area formula is the determinant of a 3×3 matrix of the coordinates, halved. Determinants therefore measure area in two dimensions and volume in three — one idea underlying both.
